title: In the news — how Indonesian journalists write and talk
goal: Read a local news article and a headline without getting lost, recognise the fixed vocabulary of reporting (*menurut, dilaporkan, pihak, terkait, sebanyak*), and answer a journalist's questions on the radio in clean, careful Indonesian.
bekal: turn a clipped headline like *Warga Keluhkan Jalan Rusak* back into a full sentence
tell who said what with *menurut*, *mengatakan*, *menyatakan* and the faceless *dilaporkan*
give numbers the way the news does: *sebanyak dua belas rumah*, *mencapai Rp90 juta*, *tujuh di antaranya*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Berita tentang Sumberwangi

notes: **Headlines have their own grammar.** Indonesian headlines drop the *me-* prefix (*Perbaiki*, not *Memperbaiki*), skip *yang* and *telah*, and capitalise every major word. It is the same economy that makes English write “Residents Repair Bridge”. Read a headline by mentally putting the prefix back: *perbaiki → memperbaiki*.

**Pascabanjir** — *pasca-* means “post-, after” and in standard spelling is written joined to the next word: *pascabanjir, pascapanen, pascasarjana* (postgraduate). You will also see it separated by a hyphen before a capital (*pasca-Lebaran*). In speech people simply say *setelah banjir*.

**Ratna (47)** — Indonesian news gives a person's age in brackets straight after the name, and often drops titles like *Bu* or *Pak*. It is not rude in print, whatever Bu Ratna thinks; saying someone's bare name to their face would be.

**Pihak** literally means “side, party”, and newsrooms use it for any institution that says something: *pihak desa* (the village authorities), *pihak kepolisian* (the police), *pihak sekolah* (the school), *pihak terkait* (the relevant parties). It lets a reporter quote an organisation without naming a person.

**Dilaporkan mencapai** — “is reported to reach”. *Dilaporkan*, *disebutkan* and *diperkirakan* are passive with no doer, which is precisely their point: the reporter does not say who reported it. Sarah's *Dilaporkan siapa?* is the right reflex for any careful reader.

**Serem** is the spoken form of *seram* (creepy, scary); *keren* is “cool”; *viral* has been borrowed straight from English. *Redaksi* is the editorial office of a paper or site — the place you send a *klarifikasi* or a *hak jawab* (right of reply).

grammars.title: Reading headlines: put the prefixes back
body: A headline is a full sentence with the grammar squeezed out. The verb loses its *me-*, the article words vanish, and a comma often replaces “after” or “in”. Rebuild it and it becomes ordinary Indonesian.

head: Headline
Full sentence
English
rows: Chilli prices rise ahead of Lebaran

after: ⚠️ *Amankan / diamankan* — “to make safe” — is the polite police word for arresting someone. *Tiga orang diamankan* means three people were taken into custody, not rescued.
*Jelang* is the headline form of *menjelang* (“ahead of, approaching”), and *terjang* (to strike, to sweep away) is a favourite verb for floods, storms and even price rises.

grammars.title: Who said it: reporting verbs
body: News Indonesian is careful about sources, and each reporting verb has a slightly different weight. *Menurut* needs no verb at all and is the easiest to use.

head: Indonesian
Weight
Example
rows: *Menurut Pak Harun, jembatan selesai bulan ini.*

after: In news prose the pronoun is *ia* rather than *dia*: *Ia mengatakan…*. Both mean “he/she”; *ia* simply sounds written.
💬 In conversation all of this collapses into *katanya* and *bilang*: *Katanya kerugiannya 150 juta* — “apparently the losses were 150 million.”

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Wawancara di radio
dialogs.intro: Three days later Sarah is a guest on a morning talk show at a Magelang community radio station. The host, Mas Aji, has read the same article.

lines.text: Pendengar setia, pagi ini kami kedatangan tamu dari Desa Sumberwangi, Mbak Sarah. Selamat pagi, Mbak.

notes: **Kami kedatangan tamu** — *kedatangan* is a *ke-an* adversative-style verb meaning “to receive a visit from”: “we have been come-to by a guest”. It is the standard way hosts open: *Hari ini kami kedatangan tamu istimewa.*

**Para pendengar** — *para* marks a plural group of people and is formal: *para pendengar, para tamu, para peserta*. Never double it with reduplication: ⚠️ *para pendengar-pendengar* is a classic error even among Indonesians.

**Beredar kabar bahwa…** — “word is going round that…”. *Beredar* (to circulate) is how journalists introduce a rumour without endorsing it. *Kabar* is news in the everyday sense; *berita* is news as a published item.

**Perlu diluruskan** — literally “needs to be straightened”. *Meluruskan* is the gentle, face-saving way to correct a public error: nobody is accused of lying, a line is just being made straight again.

**Saya tidak berwenang menjawab** — “I don't have the authority to answer.” This is Sarah declining politely and passing the question to the right *pihak*. It is a useful sentence at any press moment, and much safer than *Saya tidak tahu*.

**Jangan ke mana-mana** — “don't go anywhere”, the fixed radio and TV phrase before an ad break. *Kalau tidak ada halangan* (“if there is no obstacle”) is the formal twin of *insyaallah* for future plans.

grammars.title: Counting the way the news counts
body: News Indonesian rarely just puts a number in front of a noun. It frames it with a quantity word that makes the sentence sound measured and official.
after: *Sebanyak* sits at the front of the sentence and is followed by the number; in speech you would simply drop it: *Dua belas rumah rusak.*
Money is written *Rp90 juta* or *Rp90.000.000* — a full stop, not a comma, separates thousands, and a comma marks decimals: *2,5 juta* is two and a half million.

blocks.text: A small set of words turns up in almost every Indonesian news item. Learn these and a local news site stops looking like a wall of text.

head: Indonesian
English
Typical phrase
rows: so far / at the time of writing

blocks.text: *Tidak ada korban jiwa* — “no loss of life” — is the phrase every reader looks for first in a disaster report. *Korban* on its own can mean anyone affected, so *korban banjir* includes people whose kitchens were flooded.

sections.title: ADIKSIMBA: how a news story is built

blocks.text: Indonesian journalism students learn the English “5W + 1H” under a memorable acronym: **ADIKSIMBA** — *Apa, DI mana, Kapan, SIapa, Mengapa, BAgaimana*. A good first paragraph (*teras berita*, the lead) answers most of them.

blocks.title: Small print worth decoding
items: *Sabtu (22/4)* — the day, then the date as day/month in brackets: Saturday 22 April.
*(sar)*, *(ant)* at the end — the reporter's initials or the news agency (*Antara*).
*Baca juga:* — “read also”, a link to a related story in the middle of an article.
